parts.title: Welcome to the university library

turns.text: Hi everyone, and welcome to Hartwell Library. My name's Dana Whitmore, and I'm one of the librarians here. Over the next twenty minutes or so, I'll tell you how borrowing works, where you can study, and what kind of help you can get. So, let's start with borrowing.
turns.speaker: librarian

turns.text: Your student card is also your library card, so there's nothing extra to sign up for. Now, a lot of you will have heard that undergraduates can take out ten items at a time. That was true until last year, but the limit's now fifteen. Graduate students can have twenty, but for you, it's fifteen.
turns.speaker: librarian

turns.text: Okay, what if you keep something too long? We actually got rid of daily fines a couple of years ago, so you won't be paying a few cents a day. What happens instead is that your account gets frozen, so you can't check out anything else until the late item comes back. We'll only send you a bill for the replacement cost if something's more than six weeks overdue.
turns.speaker: librarian

turns.text: Right, course reserves. These are books your professors have put aside because the whole class needs them, and they're kept behind the main service desk. Some of you might think you can only read them inside the building. That used to be the rule, but these days you can take them out for up to four hours at a time. And you don't need to request them online or anything; just ask at the desk.
turns.speaker: librarian

turns.text: Let's move on to online resources. We subscribe to thousands of journals and e-books, and you can get to all of them from home. A few years ago, you had to install special software on your laptop to do that. Now you just sign in through the library website with the same email and password you use for everything else on campus. There's no need to register with us separately.
turns.speaker: librarian

turns.text: And if we don't have something, we can borrow it from another library for you. That's called an interlibrary loan, and it's free. Journal articles are quickest; they usually arrive by email in two or three days. Books take a bit longer, normally about a week, although something rare or very old can take up to a month.
turns.speaker: librarian

turns.text: We also run workshops all semester, on things like citing sources and searching databases. Some new students also rush to book one-on-one appointments with a librarian in their first week. But honestly, the first thing I'd ask you to do is the online orientation tutorial on our website. It only takes about twenty minutes, and it'll answer most of your questions before you even have them.
turns.speaker: librarian

turns.text: Okay, now let me tell you about some of the spaces and services you'll see as we walk around. First, the group study rooms on the third floor. You can reserve them on our website up to seven days in advance, and I'd recommend that, because they fill up fast. And there's a myth that they're only for final-year students. That's not true at all; anyone can book them.
turns.speaker: librarian

turns.text: Next, the silent reading room on the fourth floor. It's completely quiet, and to keep it that way, you're not allowed to bring bags inside. There are lockers just outside the door for that. Some people ask if it stays open all night during exams. It doesn't, I'm afraid; that's the twenty-four-hour lounge on the ground floor.
turns.speaker: librarian

turns.text: If your own laptop breaks down, don't panic. You can borrow one of ours from the service desk, using your student card. They're very popular, so the rule is they have to come back to the desk before we close that same evening. You can't keep them overnight.
turns.speaker: librarian

turns.text: Then there's the writing center, where tutors help you plan and improve your essays. If you've seen old maps of the building, they show it on the second floor. But over the summer it moved down to the basement, next to the computer lab, so that's where you'll find it now.
turns.speaker: librarian

turns.text: Printing. Printers are on every floor, and you pay with your student card. Each semester, the first hundred pages are free, so you don't pay anything until you've used those up. After that it's ten cents a page, sorry, eight cents, for black and white.
turns.speaker: librarian

turns.text: And finally, the subject librarians. Every department has one, and they're the people to talk to about research for your assignments. During the day you can drop by their offices on the first floor, but a lot of students have classes then, so they also offer video calls in the evenings, until about nine. You'll find the links on the library website.
turns.speaker: librarian

turns.text: Okay, that's the overview. Let's head upstairs, and I'll show you the third floor first.
turns.speaker: librarian

explanation.uk: Раніше ліміт для студентів бакалаврату становив "ten", але бібліотекарка каже, що тепер він "fifteen". "Twenty" — це ліміт для магістрантів і аспірантів, а не для нових студентів бакалаврату.

parts.title: A bakery case study

turns.text: Right, Callum, shall we make a start on the bakery case study? The report's due on Friday.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Yeah, good idea. I've read it twice now. Shall we begin with what Hartley's Bakery got right?
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: OK. At first I thought the loyalty card was one of their strengths, but then I noticed they gave it up after about three months, because hardly anyone used it.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Right, so that doesn't really count. What about the location? It's near the station, isn't it?
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Well, it's on a side street behind the station, so most commuters walk straight past it. If anything, I'd put that under problems.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Fair enough. And staff training? I thought they had a proper programme.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: The owner talks about wanting one, but it never actually happened. They just learn on the job.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: OK. For me, the real strength is where everything comes from. All their flour is milled about five miles away and the eggs come from a farm nearby. And then there's Instagram: the owner posts photos of the morning bake every day, and that's what brings in most new customers.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Agreed, those are the two to focus on. So, problems. The case study mentions that big supermarket that opened on the ring road last year.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Yes, but the owner says her sales hardly changed after it opened, so I don't think that's a real issue. And the online reviews are nearly all five stars, so it's not about quality either.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: No. What struck me was the bills. Running the ovens from four in the morning means their electricity costs have almost doubled in two years. And then there's how much they throw away. Around a fifth of everything they bake is still on the shelves at closing time.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: That's a lot. I'd expected them to say they couldn't find trained bakers, but apparently recruitment has been easy.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Right. So what are we going to recommend? I wondered about moving to the high street, where more people pass by.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: The rent there's three times as much, though. They'd never afford it. What about staying open into the evening?
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: That means paying staff for extra hours, and the area's pretty quiet after six. I don't think so.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: So I'd go for two things. First, replacing the old ovens with energy-efficient ones. There's a government grant that would cover half the cost. Second, selling whatever's left at the end of the day at half price, maybe through one of those food-waste apps.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Yes, that tackles both of the big problems directly. Should we suggest a marketing consultant as well?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: I don't think they need one. Their Instagram's already doing that job for free.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: True. OK, the second section is what to do with each product. Let's start with the sourdough.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.say: It's their bestseller. It sells out by eleven most mornings, and at three pounds twenty a loaf it's cheaper than anywhere else in town.
turns.text: It's their bestseller. It sells out by eleven most mornings, and at £3.20 a loaf it's cheaper than anywhere else in town.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: I was going to say they should just bake more of it, but that means more energy. I reckon they could easily charge more, and people would still buy it.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Agreed. Next, the cinnamon buns. They fly off the shelves on Saturdays and Sundays, but from Monday to Friday nearly half of them end up in the bin.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: So should they stop making them altogether?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: No, they're far too popular for that. They should just bake them for the weekend and leave them out the rest of the time.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Makes sense. Then there are the celebration cakes. At the moment you have to go into the shop to order one, and the owner admits she loses customers because of that.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: I'd thought about suggesting an advert in the local paper, but that's a bit old-fashioned. People want to choose a design and pay from home, so they should set up a way to order them through the website.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Good. Sandwiches next. They're really the part of the business that loses money. The fillings have to be bought fresh every day, there's the café next door competing, and they make about 10p on each one.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: I was going to say cut the price, but you're right, there's no point. Let's just say they should stop making them completely.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: What about the gluten-free brownies? Hardly anyone buys them in the shop.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: No, but the case study says two cafés in town have asked about stocking them. So instead of relying on the shop, they could sell them to cafés and offices in the area.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: That's better than my idea, which was just to change the packaging. And the meat pies?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: They're a bit tricky. They make thirty a day, but only about twenty get sold. They're worth keeping, but they should make fewer of them.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.say: And finally, the hot drinks. A coffee's only one pound fifty, which is about a pound less than the chains charge.
turns.text: And finally, the hot drinks. A coffee's only £1.50, which is about a pound less than the chains charge.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: I'd say leave those as they are. Actually, no. The beans come from a local roaster, so customers would happily pay a bit more. Let's put that down too.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Right. I'll write up the products section tonight and send it over tomorrow, Callum.
turns.speaker: student_a

questions.prompt: Which TWO things do the students think the bakery did well?
questions.evidence: All their flour is milled about five miles away and the eggs come from a farm nearby. And then there's Instagram: the owner posts photos of the morning bake every day

explanation.en: Callum praises the flour and eggs that come from nearby and the daily Instagram posts. The loyalty card was given up, the location is on a side street, and the staff training never happened.
explanation.ru: Callum хвалит муку и яйца от местных поставщиков и ежедневные публикации в Instagram. От карты лояльности отказались, пекарня находится на боковой улице, а обучение персонала так и не провели.
explanation.uk: Callum хвалить борошно та яйця від місцевих постачальників і щоденні дописи в Instagram. Від картки лояльності відмовилися, пекарня розташована на бічній вулиці, а навчання персоналу так і не відбулося.

explanation.uk: Булочки добре продаються в суботу й неділю, але в будні пропадають, тому Callum пропонує пекти їх лише на вихідні. Повністю відмовлятися від них він не хоче.

explanation.uk: Callum хоче, щоб клієнти могли замовляти й оплачувати покупки з дому через вебсайт. Ідею реклами в місцевій газеті він відкидає як застарілу.

questions.evidence: they should stop making them completely

explanation.en: The sandwiches lose money, so the students decide the bakery should stop making them. Cutting the price is considered but rejected.
explanation.ru: Сэндвичи приносят убытки, поэтому студенты решают, что пекарне стоит перестать их делать. Вариант снизить цену обсуждают, но отклоняют.
explanation.uk: Сендвічі збиткові, тому студенти вирішують, що пекарні варто припинити їх готувати. Варіант знизити ціну розглядають, але відкидають.

questions.evidence: they could sell them to cafés and offices in the area

explanation.en: Callum suggests selling the brownies to nearby cafés and offices. Harriet's idea of changing the packaging is rejected as less good.
explanation.ru: Callum предлагает продавать брауни ближайшим кафе и офисам. Идею Harriet изменить упаковку отклоняют как менее удачную.
explanation.uk: Callum пропонує продавати брауні найближчим кафе та офісам. Ідею Harriet змінити упаковку відкидають як менш вдалу.

questions.prompt: Meat pies
questions.evidence: They're worth keeping, but they should make fewer of them.

explanation.en: Only about twenty of the thirty pies sell each day, so they should keep the pies but make fewer.
explanation.ru: Из тридцати пирогов каждый день продаётся только около двадцати, поэтому пироги стоит оставить, но печь их меньше.
explanation.uk: З тридцяти пирогів щодня продається лише близько двадцяти, тому пироги варто залишити, але пекти їх менше.

segments.text: Part 4. You will hear a social history lecturer giving a talk about the development of the bicycle and its effects on society. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
That is the end of Part 4. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers.

parts.title: The bicycle and social change

turns.text: Good morning, everyone. Today I want to talk about something most of you probably rode as kids without a second thought: the bicycle. I'll start by tracing how its design developed during the nineteenth century. Then, since this is a social history course, we'll look at what it did to people's working lives, to women's freedom, and to the shape of our cities.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: So, let's start in Germany in 1817. A man called Karl Drais built what's usually considered the first two-wheeled machine. It had no pedals at all. You sat on it and pushed yourself along with your feet. Now, why did he bother? One popular theory is that after a run of bad harvests, oats became terribly expensive, and lots of horses died or were sold off. So Drais was looking for a way to get around without relying on one.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: The next big step came in France in the 1860s, when pedals were fixed directly to the front wheel. These machines were officially called velocipedes, but people gave them a much less flattering name. They had wooden wheels with iron rims, and the streets were often cobbled, so in English they became known as boneshakers. I think you can imagine why.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Then, in the 1870s, came the penny-farthing, with that enormous front wheel and tiny back one. People often assume the big wheel was there for comfort, but that wasn't really the point. Because the pedals turned the front wheel directly, a bigger wheel meant you travelled further with each turn of the pedals. In other words, more speed. The downside was that a fall from that height could be serious, so the riders were mostly young, athletic men.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: The real turning point was the so-called safety bicycle, which appeared in England in 1885. Its two wheels were roughly the same size, and the rider sat much lower. But the crucial change wasn't the frame. It was that the pedals now drove the back wheel by means of a chain, so you could get good speed without a giant wheel.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: A few years later, in 1887, sorry, 1888, a Scottish vet living in Belfast, John Dunlop, developed the air-filled tyre. He didn't originally have bicycles in mind, actually. He was trying to give his young son a smoother ride on his tricycle. Within a decade, though, these pneumatic tyres were standard on bicycles everywhere.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Right. So by the 1890s you had a machine that was safe, comfortable and, as factories began mass-producing them, increasingly affordable. That's when the great bicycle boom happened, and Australia was very much part of it. Let's turn to work. In the outback, shearers began riding bicycles between sheep stations, sometimes covering hundreds of kilometres. Before that, they'd have walked, or gone on horseback if they could afford a horse.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: And on the Western Australian goldfields, around Coolgardie, cyclists were paid to carry letters between the mining camps and the nearest telegraph office. People sometimes assume they carried gold, but that would've been far too risky on a bike in the middle of the desert. Letters, on the other hand, were light, and they were urgent.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.say: Now, the bicycle probably had its most dramatic effect on women's lives. To ride comfortably, many women gave up the long, heavy skirts of the time. Some wore what were called bloomers, that's B, L, O, O, M, E, R, S, which were loose trousers gathered at the knee. It was a very visible challenge to ideas about how a respectable woman should dress.
turns.text: Now, the bicycle probably had its most dramatic effect on women's lives. To ride comfortably, many women gave up the long, heavy skirts of the time. Some wore what were called bloomers, that's B-L-O-O-M-E-R-S, which were loose trousers gathered at the knee. It was a very visible challenge to ideas about how a respectable woman should dress.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: But it wasn't only about clothing. A young, unmarried woman was generally expected to have a chaperone with her whenever she went out, usually an older woman from the family who'd keep an eye on her. On a bicycle, she could simply ride off on her own, and a chaperone on foot couldn't possibly keep up. So women gained a kind of independence they'd never had before.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Not everyone approved, of course. Some church leaders complained that cycling kept people away from Sunday services, but that applied to men as much as women. The fiercest criticism of women riding came from doctors, who warned it could damage their health. Some even described a condition called bicycle face, a strained, exhausted expression. Sounds ridiculous now, but it appeared in serious medical journals.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Finally, cities. We tend to think it was the motor car that transformed our roads, but cyclists actually got there first. In the 1890s, cycling clubs in Melbourne and Sydney, and in Britain and America too, lobbied governments to build smoother, better-maintained roads. The clubs also published maps for their members, but those they produced themselves. So cars later benefited from improvements that cyclists had campaigned for.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: The other big change was where people lived. Before the bicycle, most working people had to live within walking distance of their jobs, so they crowded into the inner city. With a cheap bike, a clerk or a factory worker could live several kilometres away, out in the suburbs, where housing was cheaper and less crowded. So the bicycle helped start the outward spread of our cities, alongside the early trams, and well before the car.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Okay, that's the overview. Next week, we'll look at how the car pushed the bicycle aside for much of the twentieth century, and why it's now making a comeback.
turns.speaker: lecturer

groups.title: The History of the Bicycle and Social Change

questions.prompt: 1817, Drais's machine: may have been a response to a lack of ______ for transport
questions.evidence: lots of horses died or were sold off

explanation.en: The lecturer says many horses died or were sold, so Drais wanted a way to travel without one. Oats were expensive, but oats are not a means of transport.
explanation.ru: Лектор говорит, что многие лошади ("horses") погибли или были проданы, поэтому Drais хотел найти способ передвигаться без них. Овёс ("oats") действительно был дорогим, но овёс — не средство передвижения.
explanation.uk: Лектор каже, що багато коней ("horses") загинули або були продані, тому Drais хотів знайти спосіб пересуватися без них. Овес ("oats") справді був дорогим, але овес — не засіб пересування.

questions.prompt: 1860s French velocipede: nicknamed ______ in English
questions.evidence: so in English they became known as boneshakers

explanation.en: The official name was velocipede, but in English people called them boneshakers because of the hard wheels on cobbled streets.
explanation.ru: Официальное название было "velocipede", но по-английски их называли "boneshakers" («костотрясы») из-за жёстких колёс на булыжных мостовых.
explanation.uk: Офіційна назва була "velocipede", але англійською їх називали "boneshakers" («кістколами») через тверді колеса на бруківці.

questions.prompt: 1870s penny-farthing: large front wheel gave the rider more ______
questions.evidence: In other words, more speed.

explanation.en: The big wheel meant the bike went further with each turn of the pedals, giving more speed. The lecturer says it was not really about comfort.
explanation.ru: Благодаря большому колесу велосипед проезжал больше за каждый оборот педалей, а значит, ехал быстрее ("speed"). Лектор говорит, что дело было вовсе не в комфорте ("comfort").
explanation.uk: Завдяки великому колесу велосипед проїжджав більше за кожен оберт педалей, а отже, їхав швидше ("speed"). Лектор каже, що річ була зовсім не в комфорті ("comfort").

questions.prompt: 1885 safety bicycle: pedals linked to the back wheel by a ______
questions.evidence: the pedals now drove the back wheel by means of a chain

explanation.en: The key change was that a chain connected the pedals to the back wheel. The lecturer says the important change was not the frame.
explanation.ru: Главное изменение — цепь ("chain") соединила педали с задним колесом. Лектор говорит, что важным изменением была не рама ("frame").
explanation.uk: Головна зміна — ланцюг ("chain") з'єднав педалі із заднім колесом. Лектор каже, що важливою зміною була не рама ("frame").

questions.prompt: 1888, Dunlop's air-filled tyre: first made for his son's ______
questions.evidence: give his young son a smoother ride on his tricycle

explanation.en: Dunlop wanted his son to have a smoother ride on his tricycle. He did not first have bicycles in mind.
explanation.ru: Dunlop хотел, чтобы его сыну было мягче ездить на трёхколёсном велосипеде ("tricycle"). О двухколёсных велосипедах ("bicycles") он поначалу не думал.
explanation.uk: Dunlop хотів, щоб його синові було м'якше їздити на триколісному велосипеді ("tricycle"). Про двоколісні велосипеди ("bicycles") він спочатку не думав.

questions.prompt: Outback shearers cycled long distances between ______
questions.evidence: shearers began riding bicycles between sheep stations

explanation.en: Shearers rode bicycles from one sheep station to another. Before this they walked or used horses.
explanation.ru: Стригали овец ("shearers") ездили на велосипедах от одной овцеводческой фермы ("sheep station") к другой. До этого они ходили пешком или ездили верхом.
explanation.uk: Стригалі овець ("shearers") їздили на велосипедах від однієї вівчарської ферми ("sheep station") до іншої. До цього вони ходили пішки або їздили верхи.

questions.prompt: Cyclists on the goldfields were employed to transport ______
questions.evidence: cyclists were paid to carry letters between the mining camps

explanation.en: The cyclists carried letters, which were light and urgent. The lecturer says they did not carry gold because it was too risky.
explanation.ru: Велосипедисты возили письма ("letters") — они лёгкие и срочные. Лектор говорит, что золото ("gold") они не возили, потому что это было слишком рискованно.
explanation.uk: Велосипедисти возили листи ("letters") — вони легкі й термінові. Лектор каже, що золото ("gold") вони не возили, бо це було надто ризиковано.

questions.prompt: Some female cyclists wore ______ instead of long skirts
questions.evidence: Some wore what were called bloomers, that's B-L-O-O-M-E-R-S

explanation.en: The lecturer spells out the word bloomers, which were loose trousers gathered at the knee.
explanation.ru: Лектор произносит по буквам слово "bloomers" — так назывались свободные брюки, собранные у колена.
explanation.uk: Лектор вимовляє по літерах слово "bloomers" — так називали вільні штани, зібрані біля коліна.

questions.prompt: Young women could now go out without a ______
questions.evidence: she could simply ride off on her own, and a chaperone on foot couldn't possibly keep up

explanation.en: Young women were expected to have a chaperone, but on a bicycle they could ride away alone because the chaperone could not follow on foot.
explanation.ru: Считалось, что молодых женщин должна сопровождать компаньонка ("chaperone"), но на велосипеде они могли уехать одни: пешком компаньонка за ними не поспевала.
explanation.uk: Вважалося, що молодих жінок має супроводжувати компаньйонка ("chaperone"), але на велосипеді вони могли поїхати самі: пішки компаньйонка за ними не встигала.

questions.prompt: Strongest critics of women cycling: ______, who said it was unhealthy
questions.evidence: The fiercest criticism of women riding came from doctors

explanation.en: Doctors gave the strongest criticism and warned about women's health. Church leaders also complained, but about Sunday services, not about women in particular.
explanation.ru: Резче всех критиковали врачи ("doctors"): они предупреждали о вреде для женского здоровья. Церковные деятели ("church leaders") тоже жаловались, но их беспокоили воскресные службы, а не именно женщины.
explanation.uk: Найрізкіше критикували лікарі ("doctors"): вони попереджали про шкоду для жіночого здоров'я. Церковні діячі ("church leaders") теж скаржилися, але їх турбували недільні служби, а не саме жінки.
